pairs.task: What does a valid WebMCP Challenge submission have to include? List all deliverables and the specific requirements for the project description, demo video, and source-code repository.
pairs.answerA: Unsupported from the publicly fetched baseline pages. The challenge homepage confirms that entrants must build and deploy either a new WebMCP-enabled app or add WebMCP support to an existing app, and it links to Rules, Resources, Updates, and a Devpost submission-management page. However, the fetched Rules page exposed only its title; Resources exposed links but no submission requirements; and the relevant deadline-reminder update had no readable body. The remaining submission-management page is an authenticated flow. Therefore the full deliverable list and the specific requirements for the project description, demo video, and source-code repository cannot be established from this public fetch evidence.
pairs.answerB: A valid submission must include four deliverables: (1) a working live URL accessible to judges in ChatGPT’s in-app browser or in Google Chrome with WebMCP enabled; authenticated apps are allowed, with credentials supplied in the Submission Form; (2) a text project description explaining why the use case strongly fits WebMCP, how it improves user experience, what people and agents can do together that was previously difficult or impossible, and briefly how WebMCP was implemented; (3) a public YouTube demo video under 3 minutes, with audio, clearly showing both what was built and how WebMCP was used; and (4) a public GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket repository containing all source code, assets, and instructions needed to make the project functional, plus an open-source license file that is detectable and visible at the top of the repository page/About section. The submission page also shows the expected WebMCP tool-registration pattern in the repository guidance.

pairs.task: Can a project begun before August 25, 2026 qualify? Explain which work counts, how judges assess it, and what evidence the entrant must provide.
pairs.answerA: Yes. A project that existed before the submission period began on August 25, 2026 can qualify only if it was meaningfully extended with WebMCP after the submission period started. Judges evaluate a pre-existing project solely on the work added during the submission period, not on its earlier functionality. The entrant must clearly distinguish old work from new work and provide evidence that the WebMCP extension occurred within the period—for example, timestamped or dated commit history, or equivalent documentation.
pairs.answerB: Unsupported from the publicly fetched baseline pages. The homepage says entrants may create a new WebMCP-enabled app or add WebMCP support to an existing app, which shows that an existing application can be in scope. But it does not state whether a project begun before August 25, 2026 qualifies, which portion of its work counts, how judges assess that work, or what evidence the entrant must provide. The public Rules fetch exposed only the rules title, while the judging-related update exposed no readable body, so the requested conditions cannot be verified from this arm’s evidence.

pairs.task: Give the final extended submission deadline in PT and in EDT. Explain why it changed and identify the three project artifacts that must remain unchanged after submissions close.
pairs.answerA: The final extended deadline is Friday, September 4, 2026 at 1:00 a.m. PT, which is 4:00 a.m. EDT. It was moved 12 hours later from Thursday, September 3 at 1:00 p.m. PT because of an ongoing outage that the OpenAI team was working to fix. Once submissions close, entrants must not change the source-code repository, demo video, or live site/application; the live site must also remain online and the video must not be swapped.
pairs.answerB: Unsupported from the publicly fetched baseline pages. The Updates index establishes that there was a post titled “Deadline Extension | 12 more hours,” which supports only that the deadline was extended by 12 hours. The fetched Schedule page contained only its heading, and the extension post exposed no readable body. Consequently the final PT deadline, its EDT conversion, the reason for the change, and the three project artifacts that must remain unchanged after submissions close cannot be recovered from this baseline evidence.

pairs.task: How do the two judging stages work? Name all four equally weighted criteria in the second stage and explain the tie-breaking order.
pairs.answerA: Stage One is a pass/fail viability screen: the project must reasonably fit the challenge theme and reasonably use the required APIs/SDKs. Every submission that passes advances to Stage Two, where judges score four equally weighted criteria: (1) WebMCP Leverage—depth and skill of WebMCP use, genuine effort, and a working non-trivial implementation; (2) Execution—a working/runnable, complete and coherent product experience rather than only a technical proof of concept; (3) Potential Impact—a credible, specific real problem and audience, with the demonstrated solution actually addressing it; and (4) Creativity & Ambition—novelty, creativity, and differentiation from existing concepts. For a tie, compare tied entries on the criteria in that listed order: first WebMCP Leverage, then Execution, then Potential Impact, then Creativity & Ambition. If still tied on all four, the judging panel votes.
pairs.answerB: Unsupported from the publicly fetched baseline pages. The homepage provides only general challenge context, and the Updates index links to a post titled “2 days left, and what judges actually look for.” But the fetched Rules page yielded only its title and that judging update yielded no readable body. The two-stage judging process, all four equally weighted second-stage criteria, and the tie-breaking sequence therefore cannot be verified from this arm’s evidence.

pairs.task: How can judges test a submitted application in each supported browser environment? Include the minimum Chrome version and required flag, whether judges must open the live application, and where an entrant must provide private login credentials.
pairs.answerA: The fetched challenge homepage says judges can test the deployed app in ChatGPT’s in-app browser, where WebMCP works out of the box. For Chrome, the linked Chrome documentation says the WebMCP origin trial begins with Chrome 149; for local testing, open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, set it to Enabled, and relaunch Chrome. Judges must open the live application: that documentation says clients and browsers must visit a site directly to discover its callable tools. The private-credential placement is unsupported by this public baseline evidence: the Rules fetch exposed only its title, Resources exposed links but no relevant instructions, and the Devpost submission-management page is an authenticated flow, so I cannot verify where private login credentials must be provided.
pairs.answerB: Judges can test the live application in either (1) ChatGPT’s in-app browser, where WebMCP works by default, or (2) Google Chrome 149 or later after enabling chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and restarting Chrome. Entrants must provide a working live URL that functions in those environments and clear testing instructions. Judges are not required to build the project from source, and they are not generally required to test it, but the submission FAQ says they will visit/open the live URL directly to see how it works. A live app may be private/authenticated, but the entrant must put the necessary login credentials in the Devpost Submission Form (with the testing instructions) so judges can access it.
